text: Lipschitz stability for identification of piecewise constant conductivity coefficient in parabolic equation from finitely many interior or boundary measurements The theorem establishes a stability estimate for the difference between two conductivity functions in a domain. It bounds the L-infinity norm of their difference on an inner subdomain by a sum of boundary differences and solution differences raised to a fractional power. The constants depend on domain parameters, boundary data, and operator coefficients. Under analytic boundary and coefficient conditions, the estimate holds on the entire domain. For a Lipschitz domain with given parameters, if the L2 norm difference of two weak solutions on a boundary part is bounded by epsilon, then the L-infinity norm difference of the corresponding coefficients on a specific inner boundary region is bounded by a function of epsilon. This function is the composition of eta with itself applied to epsilon. The result establishes a stability estimate for the coefficients based on the solutions' proximity. The difference between two piecewise constant functions is bounded by a constant times the difference between their Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps. This bound holds in the infinity norm for the functions and in the operator norm for the maps. The conductivity is uniquely determined by its Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. The relationship is Lipschitz continuous. The theorem applies to a bounded Lipschitz domain with certain coefficient functions. It assumes specific boundary conditions and right-hand side functionals. There exists a stability constant independent of the forcing terms. This constant bounds the solutions of the given equations.

title: Theorem 1.3 — Conditional Stability for Single Interior Measurement
text: The theorem establishes a stability estimate for the difference between two conductivity functions in a domain. It bounds the L-infinity norm of their difference on an inner subdomain by a sum of boundary differences and solution differences raised to a fractional power. The constants depend on domain parameters, boundary data, and operator coefficients. Under analytic boundary and coefficient conditions, the estimate holds on the entire domain. {\rm (Main Theorem)} {\it Let $d > 0$ and $\Omega _d := \{ x \in \Omega \, :\,  \operatorname {dist}(x,\,  \mathbb {R}^n \setminus \Omega ) > d\} $. Let $\gamma _1, \gamma _2$ be an admissible pair and $A, \rho , \gamma _1, \gamma _2, \omega ^2$ satisfy Assumptions 1,2,3, with $||A||_{W^{1,\infty }(\Omega )} \le \sigma ^{-1}$ and $||\gamma _k||_{W^{1,\infty }(\Omega )} \le \sigma ^{-1},\,  k=1,2$. Then there exist constants $C>0$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$ depending only on $\Omega $, $d$, $\sigma $, $g_1$ and the coefficients of $L_1$ such that \begin{equation}  \Vert \gamma _2-\gamma _1\Vert _{L^\infty (\Omega _d)} \le C\left(\Vert \gamma _2-\gamma _1\Vert _{L^\infty (\partial \Omega )} +\Vert u_2-u_1\Vert _{W^{2,1}(\Omega )}\right)^\alpha \end{equation} for any $g_2$ and $\gamma _2$ of an admissible pair $(\gamma _1,\,  \gamma _2)$. Furthermore, if $\Omega $ has an analytic smooth boundary and if $g_1$ is analytic in $\partial \Omega $ and all the coefficients of $L_1$ are analytic near $\partial \Omega $, then we have the estimate} (\ref{eq::stability}) {\emph in which $L^\infty (\Omega _d)$ is replaced with $L^\infty (\Omega )$.}\\

title: TheoremSearch: uniqueness and Lipschitz stability for recovering piecewise constant conductivity coefficient in one
text: uniqueness and Lipschitz stability for recovering piecewise constant conductivity coefficient in one-dimensional parabolic equation from interior point observations The inverse Robin problem for parabolic equations is locally Lipschitz stable. If the solution is bounded below by a positive constant on the inner boundary over time, then the difference in solutions on the accessible boundary controls the difference in Robin coefficients. This holds for all coefficients in a neighborhood of a given coefficient. The stability constant depends on the lower bound and the neighborhood size. Under certain smoothness and support conditions on the initial data, and with given functions satisfying continuity and non-vanishing properties, the inverse problem has a unique solution. The coefficient function is continuous on the time interval. The assumptions ensure the associated equation is uniformly parabolic. Under given conditions, the unique solution to the parabolic equation with initial condition linear in x is Lipschitz continuous in both time and space. The Lipschitz constant depends on the slope parameter theta. This constant is given by a function kappa of theta, which is locally bounded. The result holds for all real values of theta. For a constant p between 1 and infinity, assume the coefficients a are continuous with specified moduli of continuity on different parts of the domain. For any f in L_p, there exists a unique strong solution u in the Sobolev space W^{1,2}_p to the given parabolic equation with zero Dirichlet boundary condition. The solution satisfies an estimate where its norm is bounded by a constant times the norm of f. The constant depends only on the dimension, p, the ellipticity constant, and the moduli of continuity.

title: TheoremSearch: Bernstein-von Mises or asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood / posterior mean for nonlinear in
text: Bernstein-von Mises or asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood / posterior mean for nonlinear inverse problems with small Gaussian noise and finite-dimensional parameter Under certain assumptions, the posterior distribution converges to a normal distribution as the sample size increases. The normal distribution is centered at the maximum likelihood estimator and has a covariance matrix based on the Fisher information. This convergence holds in total variation norm. The result is known as the Bernstein-von Mises theorem. The Bernstein-von Mises theorem centered at the generalized Bayes posterior mean states that under certain regularity conditions, the posterior distribution converges to a normal distribution. This convergence occurs in total variation as the sample size goes to infinity. The limiting distribution has mean zero and covariance matrix equal to the inverse of the Hessian matrix at the true parameter. The prior density must be strictly positive and continuous near the true parameter value. Using the Laplace approximation as a prior in a Bayesian inverse problem yields a Gaussian posterior distribution. The posterior has a specific mean and covariance matrix. All moments of this posterior exist. As the noise parameter approaches zero, the posterior converges to a Gaussian centered at the maximum likelihood estimate with covariance given by the inverse of the Fisher information matrix. The posterior mean converges to the maximum likelihood estimator scaled by the noise level. This convergence holds in probability as the noise approaches zero. The result applies to functions satisfying specific regularity conditions. Consequently, the posterior mean can substitute for the estimator in the referenced theorem.

title: TheoremSearch: Lipschitz stability for identifying piecewise constant conductivity in parabolic equation from finit
text: Lipschitz stability for identifying piecewise constant conductivity in parabolic equation from finitely many interior point measurements The theorem establishes a stability estimate for the difference between two conductivity functions in a domain. It bounds the L-infinity norm of their difference on an inner subdomain by a sum of boundary differences and solution differences raised to a fractional power. The constants depend on domain parameters, boundary data, and operator coefficients. Under analytic boundary and coefficient conditions, the estimate holds on the entire domain. The difference between two piecewise constant functions is bounded by a constant times the difference between their Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps. This bound holds in the infinity norm for the functions and in the operator norm for the maps. The conductivity is uniquely determined by its Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. The relationship is Lipschitz continuous. Under given conditions, the unique solution to the parabolic equation with initial condition linear in x is Lipschitz continuous in both time and space. The Lipschitz constant depends on the slope parameter theta. This constant is given by a function kappa of theta, which is locally bounded. The result holds for all real values of theta. A bounded Lipschitz domain in the plane has a conductivity function with certain regularity and positive real part. If the relative jump in conductivity across the interface is sufficiently small, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map uniquely determines the conductivity. This holds at any proper admissible point within the domain.

title: TheoremSearch: convergence of Levenberg-Marquardt or Gauss-Newton for finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares pa
text: convergence of Levenberg-Marquardt or Gauss-Newton for finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares parameter identification with locally Lipschitz stable forward map The Gauss-Newton method converges to a solution for a nonlinear least squares problem under certain conditions. The method is well-defined and the sequence remains within a ball around the solution. The convergence rate is bounded by an expression involving the initial error and a function f. The radius of convergence is optimal under additional equality conditions, and the solution is unique under a further hypothesis. If the matrix derivative of S at nu-hat is injective, then the Gauss-Newton algorithm converges locally. If the derivative is also Lipschitz continuous, then the convergence becomes locally quadratic. Under certain assumptions on the Jacobian mapping, gradient descent with a specific step size applied to a non-linear least squares problem yields geometric convergence of the residual. The residuals of the original and linearized problems remain close throughout all iterations. The parameters of both problems also stay close to each other. Additionally, the parameters remain within a bounded distance from the initial point. For a fixed matrix A, assume a local least squares solution exists for the mapping g with an injective derivative. There is a neighborhood and constants such that the pseudoinverse norm is bounded and the mapping satisfies a Lipschitz-like condition. Under an additional bound on the pseudoinverse difference, the Gauss-Newton iteration converges linearly to the solution from all initial points in a specific region. The convergence rate is less than one and depends on the initial distance.

title: TheoremSearch: convergence of Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation
text: convergence of Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with finite-dimensional parameters, local convergence radius and asymptotic efficiency achieving Cramer-Rao bound The weighted least squares estimates for parameters a and eta are asymptotically efficient. Their scaled estimation errors converge in distribution to normal random vectors. The asymptotic covariance matrices equal the Cramer-Rao lower bounds multiplied by the noise variance. This efficiency holds for both parameter vectors under the given conditions. Under certain assumptions and moment bounds, the squared distance between the parameter estimate and the optimum almost surely converges at a rate of the natural logarithm of the sample size divided by the sample size. If the Hessian of the objective function is locally Lipschitz near the optimum and a moment exponent is at least two, the normalized estimation error converges in distribution to a normal distribution. The asymptotic covariance matrix depends on the inverse Hessian and a noise covariance term. The asymptotic variance of the estimator reaches the Cramér-Rao lower bound for all regular and unbiased estimators of the parameter. This implies that the estimator is asymptotically efficient. Under certain conditions, a local minimizer exists with high probability. This minimizer's estimated parameter converges in probability to the true parameter. The convergence holds under two different norms defined by the matrices Gamma_n and Gamma. The estimation error becomes arbitrarily small as the sample size increases.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Bounded LM posterior-mean inversion through the exact forward model approaches the Cramér–Rao floor
text: Per-sample bounded Levenberg–Marquardt on F(k), started from several points in log k and followed by an importance-sampled posterior mean under the uniform box prior, will reach val rel_l2 < 0.035. That is under twice the CRB floor of 0.0185 and well below the 0.05 success threshold. The data misfit should land near the noise level, with ||r||^2/(m sigma^2) ≈ 1. The model is fully specified. The forward map is explicit finite differences on 40 nodes over 200 steps, so it is a polynomial in k and therefore C^infinity. Noise is known Gaussian with sigma 1e-3, and there are only 4 parameters. Fisher condition numbers (median 62) indicate a well-posed local problem, so MLE through F should be nearly efficient. k1 and k4 are the weakly determined parameters (CRB rel std about 2%). They often lie near the box bounds [0.5, 2], where the MLE is biased by clipping. The posterior mean under the box prior is the Bayes estimator for squared error and handles this truncation. Working in log k improves conditioning because sensitivity scales roughly like 1/k, and it also enforces positivity. context.forward is the same discretisation that generated the data, so there is no model error the explicit scheme is stable for all k in [0.5, 2], i.e. dt*kmax/dx^2 <= 1/2 the misfit landscape in log k has a dominant basin and few spurious local minima, so 4 starts suffice the Laplace approximation is a good enough proposal for importance sampling at noise 1e-3

assumptions: context.forward is the same discretisation that generated the data, so there is no model error
the explicit scheme is stable for all k in [0.5, 2], i.e. dt*kmax/dx^2 <= 1/2
the misfit landscape in log k has a dominant basin and few spurious local minima, so 4 starts suffice
the Laplace approximation is a good enough proposal for importance sampling at noise 1e-3
data.falsifiable_test: Run on val and compute rel_l2, plus the per-sample normalized misfit ||F(k_hat)-y||^2/(m sigma^2). The hypothesis is refuted if rel_l2 >= 0.035, or if more than 5% of samples have normalized misfit > 2, which would indicate local minima or non-convergence.
data.if_fails: If misfits are at noise level but the error is large, the estimator or prior handling is at fault, e.g. a poor Laplace approximation near the bounds; switch to the mode estimator. If misfits are large, there is nonconvexity, so a learned initializer is needed (proposal 2). If misfits are large for all samples, there is forward-model mismatch.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Learned amortised initializer plus short LM refinement beats both pure regression and cold-start LM at lower cost
text: A noise-augmented MLP maps sensor traces to k with val rel_l2 of about 0.05–0.08. That is limited by finite training data (3000 samples) and amortisation error, not by information content. Using it to initialise 10 LM iterations through F will cut val rel_l2 by at least 40% relative to the MLP alone. The result should be at least as good as cold-start multistart LM, because the initialiser lies inside the correct basin. The pure ML inverse is a smooth nonlinear 4-output regression of a roughly 800-dimensional input. A neural net can learn it approximately but will not reach the CRB with n=3000. Newton-type refinement converges locally quadratically/linearly once it is inside the basin. The amortised estimate supplies that basin location and removes the dependence on multistart for k1 and k4, which are the least determined segments and where cold starts are most likely to stall. This tests whether the error budget is dominated by globalisation (basin finding) or by local statistical efficiency. training on simulated data from the same prior is allowed, and the train/val distribution matches the forward model noise augmentation at sigma=1e-3 makes the network robust to the observation noise the MLP error (about 5–8%) lies within the LM basin of attraction

noise augmentation at sigma=1e-3 makes the network robust to the observation noise
the MLP error (about 5–8%) lies within the LM basin of attraction
data.falsifiable_test: Report val rel_l2 for the MLP initializer alone and after refinement, plus the fraction of samples whose refinement moved them out of the initial basin (final misfit > 2× noise level). The hypothesis is refuted if refinement improves rel_l2 by < 40% over the initializer, or if the hybrid is worse than the best physics arm by more than 0.005.
data.if_fails: If refinement gives a small gain, the MLP is already near-efficient or LM is stuck. Compare against the proposal-1 misfit to tell which. If the hybrid is worse than cold LM, the MLP initialisations are biased into wrong basins for k1/k4, which means the misfit landscape is multimodal and globalisation should come from multistart rather than amortisation.

author: researcher-ml
title: Learned initializer + few LM steps through the forward model reaches near the Cramér–Rao floor
text: A torch_mlp trained on simulated data, refined per sample by 8 bounded Levenberg–Marquardt iterations in log-k space, will reach val rel_l2 <= 0.03. That is within about 1.6x of the CRB floor of 0.0185. A posterior-mean estimator will not be worse than the mode by more than 5% relative. The learned map supplies a basin-correct start, so the refinement removes the network's approximation bias. Only the noise-limited error should remain. The Fisher condition number is moderate (median 62) and per-parameter CR std is at most 2.2%. The posterior should therefore be sharply concentrated and nearly Gaussian at sigma=1e-3. In that regime local Gauss–Newton refinement from a good start should be close to efficient. A pure learned map with 3000 samples will likely carry approximation bias above the noise floor, especially for the weakly determined k1 and k4. The forward model is cheap (40 grid points, 200 explicit steps), so a few LM iterations per sample fit the budget. Log transform enforces positivity and evens out the curvature across [0.5, 2]. The MLP initializer lands inside the basin of the global minimiser for most samples. Multimodality is not expected given the moderate condition number, but this is unverified. The harness forward model in context.forward matches the data-generating simulator exactly: same grid, time steps and sensor indices. 8 LM iterations on 750 val samples fit within the 120 s per-experiment limit on 6 workers. Posterior concentration means the box-prior truncation matters only for samples with k near 0.5 or 2.0.

assumptions: The MLP initializer lands inside the basin of the global minimiser for most samples. Multimodality is not expected given the moderate condition number, but this is unverified.
The harness forward model in context.forward matches the data-generating simulator exactly: same grid, time steps and sensor indices.
8 LM iterations on 750 val samples fit within the 120 s per-experiment limit on 6 workers.
Posterior concentration means the box-prior truncation matters only for samples with k near 0.5 or 2.0.
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid against its own initializer alone, and against the 0.0185 CRB floor. The hypothesis is refuted if the hybrid's val rel_l2 > 0.03, or if refinement improves the initializer by less than 30% relative. Also check per-parameter errors: a k1 or k4 error far above its CR std (0.0215, 0.0174) would point to bad basins or forward mismatch.
data.if_fails: If refinement does not help, either the forward model does not match the data simulator, or the noise-limited floor is not reachable with this budget. If the hybrid is good but far from the CRB on k1 and k4 only, the end-segment posteriors are non-Gaussian or prior-truncated. That would justify estimator='posterior_mean'.

author: researcher-ml
title: Pure learned inverse map with log-conductivity targets and PCA compression meets the 0.05 success threshold without the forward model at inference
text: The map from noisy sensor time series to log k is smooth and low-dimensional. A torch_mlp on standardised, PCA-compressed raw features with log targets, trained on 3000 samples, will reach val rel_l2 < 0.05. The same configuration without PCA (pca=0) should be worse by at least 10% relative, because of noise-dominated directions in the 800-D feature space. The forward map is smooth in k and diffusive, so the observation manifold is a smooth 4-D surface in roughly 800-D space. Most variance should be captured by a few tens of principal components. The trailing components are mainly i.i.d. noise at 1e-3, and PCA removes them, which reduces input variance for a small-data MLP. Log targets linearise the roughly multiplicative effect of k on diffusion timescales. This is the cheapest route to the success criterion and serves as the data-driven reference for the hybrid. The signal subspace has dimension below 48, so PCA-48 retains essentially all identifiable information. 3000 training samples are enough for an MLP to learn a 4-output smooth map to within about 2.5x the CRB. Approximation error is roughly uniform over the box, with no severe degradation near the bounds.

assumptions: The signal subspace has dimension below 48, so PCA-48 retains essentially all identifiable information.
3000 training samples are enough for an MLP to learn a 4-output smooth map to within about 2.5x the CRB.
Approximation error is roughly uniform over the box, with no severe degradation near the bounds.
data.falsifiable_test: The hypothesis is refuted if val rel_l2 >= 0.05. The secondary claim is refuted if a pca=0 rerun is within 10% relative of the pca=32 result.
data.if_fails: The learned map's error is dominated by approximation bias, not noise. That would show physics refinement (proposal 1) is necessary rather than optional. It would also suggest that more simulated training data from context.forward is the next lever.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Prior-mean-initialised LM in log-space reaches near the CRB floor: a likelihood-limited, not model-limited, regime
text: With sigma=0.001 Gaussian noise and Fisher condition ~62, the per-sample likelihood is sharply peaked and near-Gaussian in log k, so a bounded Levenberg-Marquardt MLE/MAP in log-space with a few multistarts attains val rel_l2 within ~1.5x of the CRB floor (0.0185), i.e. <= 0.03, beating every purely data-driven library model trained on 3000 samples. Forward model is available and exactly matches the data-generating simulator (same explicit FD, 40 nodes, 200 steps), so there is no simulation-fidelity gap. The CRB diagnostic says information is sufficient for ~2% relative error; with only 4 parameters, a local Gauss-Newton method should be near-efficient if the cost surface has no spurious minima. Log transform respects positivity and makes the scale-type parameter k more uniform in sensitivity. Harness simulator used for training/val data is the same as context.forward (no model mismatch). Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=0.001, so least-squares = MLE. The misfit landscape over [0.5,2]^4 has a single basin or few basins reachable with 4 starts. Explicit FD scheme remains stable for k up to 2 (CFL satisfied by harness).

assumptions: Harness simulator used for training/val data is the same as context.forward (no model mismatch).
Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=0.001, so least-squares = MLE.
The misfit landscape over [0.5,2]^4 has a single basin or few basins reachable with 4 starts.
Explicit FD scheme remains stable for k up to 2 (CFL satisfied by harness).
data.falsifiable_test: Compute val rel_l2 and the per-parameter relative error; compare with CRB std. Hypothesis falsified if val rel_l2 > 0.03, or if errors show heavy tails (e.g., >2% of samples with relative error >0.2) indicating local minima rather than noise-limited error.
data.if_fails: If heavy-tailed errors: multimodality/poor starts -> motivates hybrid learned initialiser. If uniformly elevated error: forward/data mismatch or noise model misspecification -> inspect residual whiteness on val.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Controlled comparison: learned initialiser + short LM refinement vs. MLE; posterior-mean vs. mode tests whether box-prior bias matters at the boundaries
text: A torch_mlp initialiser (trained on simulated data with noise augmentation) followed by 15 LM iterations in log-space and MMSE posterior-mean estimation lowers val rel_l2 relative to pure MLE by >=10%, mainly by reducing errors for k near the box bounds (0.5 or 2.0) and for poorly determined k1/k4, because the posterior mean under the uniform prior shrinks the least-identified directions; the MLP alone will be worse than 0.05. Testable competing explanation for residual error after MLE: (a) noise-limited variance (posterior mean helps a bit, MSE-optimal under prior), vs (b) optimisation failure (initialiser helps). The rel_l2 metric is MSE-like, so the MMSE estimator under the true prior is the Bayes-optimal target; MLE is not. Noise augmentation matches training distribution to observed noisy features. Training data noise has the same distribution as val/test (sigma=0.001 Gaussian). Laplace approximation is adequate for importance-sampling posterior mean at this noise level. The MLP trained on 3000 samples gives an initial guess inside the correct basin.

assumptions: Training data noise has the same distribution as val/test (sigma=0.001 Gaussian).
Laplace approximation is adequate for importance-sampling posterior mean at this noise level.
The MLP trained on 3000 samples gives an initial guess inside the correct basin.
data.falsifiable_test: Compare against the pure-physics MLE arm on the same val split: hypothesis falsified if hybrid rel_l2 is not >=10% lower than best_physics. Secondary check: stratify val errors by whether any true k is within 0.1 of a bound; the predicted gain should be concentrated in that stratum. Also report MLP-only init error (expected > 0.05) as a control.
data.if_fails: If no gain over MLE: residual error is noise-limited and near-efficient; further effort should go to estimator choice only marginally. If worse than MLE: Laplace/IS posterior mean poorly calibrated near box bounds or initialiser lands in wrong basins.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Learned initializer plus LM refinement with posterior-mean output, since rel_l2 rewards MMSE rather than MLE
text: A hybrid estimator gets val rel_l2 <= 0.03. It starts from an ML regressor, runs bounded LM refinement in log-k space, then reports the box-prior posterior mean instead of the mode. The prediction is that it beats the same pipeline with estimator=mode by at least 5% relative, and the gain should concentrate in k1 and k4. The usual framing treats the inverse problem as finding the MLE. The metric, however, is a squared-error average over prior draws, and the Bayes-optimal estimator for that is the posterior mean. The diagnostics put the CRB rel_l2 floor at about 0.0185. The least-determined parameters, k1 and k4 (CRB rel std about 2%), sit near the Dirichlet ends where the signal is weak. For draws near the bounds 0.5 or 2.0, a box-truncated Laplace posterior pulls the estimate inward. That cuts MSE below what an unbiased MLE can achieve, so in principle it can even go below the CRB, which only bounds unbiased estimators. The learned initializer avoids LM getting stuck in the wrong basin, and a condition number of about 62 suggests the problem is locally well posed, so 10-20 Gauss-Newton iterations should converge. The forward model in the harness is the same simulator that generated the data, so there is no model misspecification. The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=1e-3 as stated, so the Laplace or Gauss-Newton posterior is approximately correct. The ML initializer lands inside the LM basin of attraction for most samples. Per-sample LM over 750 val samples (plus test) fits within the 120 s per-experiment limit, given that one explicit FD forward solve on a 40x200 grid is cheap.

assumptions: The forward model in the harness is the same simulator that generated the data, so there is no model misspecification.
The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=1e-3 as stated, so the Laplace or Gauss-Newton posterior is approximately correct.
The ML initializer lands inside the LM basin of attraction for most samples.
Per-sample LM over 750 val samples (plus test) fits within the 120 s per-experiment limit, given that one explicit FD forward solve on a 40x200 grid is cheap.
data.falsifiable_test: The hypothesis is rejected if either of these holds: val rel_l2 > 0.03, or the identical spec with estimator=mode is within 5% (relative) of the posterior_mean result. Per-parameter errors for k1 and k4 should show the largest mean-vs-mode gap.
data.if_fails: If mode does as well as mean, the posterior is effectively Gaussian and interior, and the metric is limited by noise (CRB). If both are above 0.03, either the initializer misses basins or there is forward-model mismatch. Compare the LM residual norm with the expected noise level, sqrt(n_obs)*sigma, to tell which.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Log-temperature features as a heat-kernel (Varadhan-type) linearisation make a kernel method competitive without any forward solves
text: A purely data-driven method reaches val rel_l2 < 0.05 with no forward-model calls at test time: RBF kernel ridge on log-transformed sensor temperatures, with noise augmentation. The log features should beat raw features by at least 20% relative at matched hyperparameters. The framing assumption to challenge is that physics refinement is needed to reach 0.05. For a Gaussian pulse diffusing through a medium, log u(x,t) behaves roughly like -d(x)^2/(4 k_eff t) plus lower-order terms (short-time heat-kernel asymptotics). Arrival-time and decay information therefore enters log u almost linearly in 1/k, while raw u is strongly nonlinear in k. With only 4 parameters and 3000 training samples, a smooth kernel interpolant in a near-linearised feature space should approach the noise floor. Noise augmentation helps because the log amplifies noise at small temperatures, and training on noisy copies teaches the regressor to down-weight those features. Sensor temperatures stay sufficiently positive over the window, or the harness's 'log' feature handles near-zero values safely. The inverse map from the 4 parameters to the data is smooth enough that 3000 samples cover the 4-D prior box densely for RBF interpolation (about 7-8 points per axis). The harness's noise_aug draws noise at the true sigma (noise_scale=1.0).

assumptions: Sensor temperatures stay sufficiently positive over the window, or the harness's 'log' feature handles near-zero values safely.
The inverse map from the 4 parameters to the data is smooth enough that 3000 samples cover the 4-D prior box densely for RBF interpolation (about 7-8 points per axis).
The harness's noise_aug draws noise at the true sigma (noise_scale=1.0).
data.falsifiable_test: Train the identical kernel_ridge config with features='raw' and with features='log', and compare val rel_l2. The hypothesis is rejected if the log variant has val rel_l2 >= 0.05, or if it is not at least 20% better than raw.
data.if_fails: If log does not beat raw, the heat-kernel linearisation intuition does not carry over to this finite-window, multi-segment, Dirichlet geometry, or the near-zero readings dominate. If it beats raw but stays above 0.05, the amortized approach is limited by sample density. That would argue for hybrid refinement (proposal 1) or a forward-model-generated larger training set as the route to the target.

author: research-critic
title: critique r1 of Bounded LM posterior-mean inversion through the exact forward model approaches the Cramér–Rao floor
text: The 0.0185 CRB figure is a local, unbiased-estimator floor taken at median Fisher information. The posterior mean is computed in log k, but the prior is uniform in k. In log coordinates the prior density is proportional to k. author: literature
title: Theorem 3 — Information and estimation in Fokker-Planck channels
text: The Bayesian Cramér-Rao bound provides a lower bound on the mean squared error of any estimator. The bound depends on the prior distribution and the conditional distribution of the data. It is expressed in terms of two information quantities: the Bayesian information and the conditional Bayesian information. The inequality holds for any estimator of the parameter.  [Proof in Appendix~\ref {AppVanTrees}] Consider a parameterized family of distributions $\{p_{Y|X}(\,\cdot \,|\, x)\}$ with prior $p_X(x)$. For any estimator $T(y)$ of $x$, \begin {align*} \mathbb{E} \left [\frac {1}{b(X)} (T(Y)-X)^2 \right ] \ge \frac {1}{\Phi _b(Y|X) + J_b(X)} = \frac {1}{J_b(X|Y)}. \end {align*}

author: researcher-ml
title: TheoremSearch: Iteration-wise rel_l2 and misfit for LM iterations 0..8 on val
text: Iteration-wise rel_l2 and misfit for LM iterations 0..8 on val The time-averages of the LALM iterates with simple relaxation satisfy an error bound that decreases with the number of iterations. The bound consists of three constants that depend on initial conditions and parameters. The first two constants relate to the distance between the initial guess and a minimizer. The third constant depends on the relaxation parameter and initial dual variable errors. For any fixed positive lambda, the data fitting error from the iteration does not increase with each step. The squared error after M iterations is bounded above by a term involving lambda, M, the L2 norm of the gradient of the minimizer, the domain measure, and the squared error level. This bound decreases as the number of iterations M increases. The sequence generated by LMTR with p equals zero has a bound on the norm of d_k in terms of the norm of h at x_k. The norm of h at the next iterate is bounded by a function of the current norm, the gradient of h, and the step d_k. This bound includes terms involving the squared norm of d_k, the Lipschitz constant L, and the parameter mu hat_k. The inequality shows how the residual norm evolves between iterations. The function value decreases at each iteration. The decrease is at least proportional to the squared norm of the change in the variable X. The constant of proportionality is L divided by two. This holds for all iterations starting from zero.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Bounded LM posterior-mean inversion through the exact forward model (paired with P-005 mode arm)
text: On the full val set, bounded LM in log k with 4 starts and 40 iterations, followed by an importance-sampled posterior mean, achieves rel_l2 < 0.025. More than 95% of samples will have normalized misfit ||F(k_hat)-y||^2/(m σ^2) < 1.5. Against the identically configured mode estimator (P-005), the posterior mean will improve rel_l2 by 0–5%, with the gain concentrated in samples with k1 or k4 within 0.1 of a bound. The pilot already places this estimator at the CRB estimate (0.0184 on n = 60), with calibrated uncertainty (z_rms 1.00) and noise-level misfit (chi2 0.94). The remaining scientific question is no longer feasibility. It is whether the Bayes estimator under the box prior adds anything over the MLE. The critic's arithmetic predicts under 5%, since CRB std is about 2% and the box width is 1.5, so few posteriors are truncated. Matching iterations and starts to P-005 makes that comparison unconfounded. Tested: context.forward matches the data generator (residual std at truth 0.000995 vs 0.001) The 60-sample pilot is representative of the 750 val samples (standard error of rel_l2 at n = 60 is roughly ±0.002) The Laplace proposal is adequate (pilot ESS 58/128)

assumptions: Tested: context.forward matches the data generator (residual std at truth 0.000995 vs 0.001)
The 60-sample pilot is representative of the 750 val samples (standard error of rel_l2 at n = 60 is roughly ±0.002)
The Laplace proposal is adequate (pilot ESS 58/128)
data.falsifiable_test: Run on the full val set and compute rel_l2 and the per-sample normalized misfit. Refuted if rel_l2 >= 0.025, or if more than 5% of samples have normalized misfit > 1.5. For the paired test against P-005 (same starts and iterations), the posterior-mean claim is refuted if the gain is negative by more than 0.0005, or if it is not concentrated in near-bound samples.
data.if_fails: If misfits are at noise level but rel_l2 is ≥ 0.025, the 60-sample pilot was optimistic and the estimator is information-limited near 0.02. Compare against the oracle-start LM. author: researcher-mathematical
title: Explicit Bayes estimator for per-sample relative loss: LM with mirrored start plus importance sampling using the correct uniform-in-k prior Jacobian
text: This custom solver uses three explicit ingredients: (i) a mirrored second start z[:, ::-1] to probe the symmetric spurious basin; (ii) importance weights that include the uniform-in-k prior density ∝ exp(sum z) in log coordinates; (iii) the Bayes-optimal point estimate for per-sample relative squared loss, k_hat = E[k/||k||^2] / E[1/||k||^2]. With these, it reaches val rel_l2 < 0.022 and lies within ±0.0005 of P-001 or better. It also provides two diagnostics. If the mirrored start wins (lower misfit than the centre start) on more than 1% of samples, a spurious mirrored basin exists. If dropping the Jacobian term changes rel_l2 by more than 0.0005, the critic's bias concern is material. The critic raised three issues that the black-box physics arm cannot answer: whether the log-Jacobian is included, whether a mirrored basin exists (the initial condition is symmetric and sensors 5/35 are nearly, but not exactly, mirror images), and which estimator is Bayes-optimal for rel_l2. Writing the solver explicitly makes each a measurable quantity. The forward map is polynomial in k, so finite-difference Jacobians in z with step 1e-4 are accurate to O(1e-8), far below the noise level of 1e-3. context.forward(theta) returns noise-free observations in the same layout as the feature vector X (supported by the harness fit report at truth) rel_l2 is computed per sample as ||k_hat-k||/||k|| and then averaged; if it is pooled instead, the estimator is still near-optimal because ||k|| varies modestly over the box Laplace proposal inflated by 1.2x gives adequate ESS (pilot ESS 58/128 for the uninflated version)

author: researcher-ml
title: Learned initializer + few LM steps through the forward model reaches near the Cramér–Rao floor
text: A torch_mlp trained on simulated data, refined per sample by 8 bounded Levenberg–Marquardt iterations in log-k space, will reach val rel_l2 <= 0.03. That is within about 1.6x of the CRB floor of 0.0185. A posterior-mean estimator will not be worse than the mode by more than 5% relative. The learned map supplies a basin-correct start, so the refinement removes the network's approximation bias. Only the noise-limited error should remain. The Fisher condition number is moderate (median 62) and per-parameter CR std is at most 2.2%. The posterior should therefore be sharply concentrated and nearly Gaussian at sigma=1e-3. In that regime local Gauss–Newton refinement from a good start should be close to efficient. A pure learned map with 3000 samples will likely carry approximation bias above the noise floor, especially for the weakly determined k1 and k4. The forward model is cheap (40 grid points, 200 explicit steps), so a few LM iterations per sample fit the budget. Log transform enforces positivity and evens out the curvature across [0.5, 2]. The MLP initializer lands inside the basin of the global minimiser for most samples. Multimodality is not expected given the moderate condition number, but this is unverified. The harness forward model in context.forward matches the data-generating simulator exactly: same grid, time steps and sensor indices. 8 LM iterations on 750 val samples fit within the 120 s per-experiment limit on 6 workers. Posterior concentration means the box-prior truncation matters only for samples with k near 0.5 or 2.0. noise model (from the simulator): additive i.i.d. Gaussian on every sensor reading; the likelihood must match it The basin-correctness of the MLP start is untested. Measure it directly as the fraction of samples with final normalized misfit below 1.5.

author: researcher-ml
title: Pure learned inverse map with log-conductivity targets and PCA compression meets the 0.05 success threshold without the forward model at inference
text: The map from noisy sensor time series to log k is smooth and low-dimensional. A torch_mlp on standardised, PCA-compressed raw features with log targets, trained on 3000 samples, will reach val rel_l2 < 0.05. The same configuration without PCA (pca=0) should be worse by at least 10% relative, because of noise-dominated directions in the 800-D feature space. The forward map is smooth in k and diffusive, so the observation manifold is a smooth 4-D surface in roughly 800-D space. Most variance should be captured by a few tens of principal components. The trailing components are mainly i.i.d. noise at 1e-3, and PCA removes them, which reduces input variance for a small-data MLP. Log targets linearise the roughly multiplicative effect of k on diffusion timescales. This is the cheapest route to the success criterion and serves as the data-driven reference for the hybrid. The signal subspace has dimension below 48, so PCA-48 retains essentially all identifiable information. 3000 training samples are enough for an MLP to learn a 4-output smooth map to within about 2.5x the CRB. Approximation error is roughly uniform over the box, with no severe degradation near the bounds. Instead of 'signal subspace < 48', test the effective signal rank directly. Compute the SVD of the noiseless Jacobian stack, or the PCA spectrum of F(k) evaluated without noise.

title: Box-bounded multistart LM-MLE in log-space is noise-limited: full-val rel_l2 within ~1.35x of the CRB floor, with no mirrored or spurious basins

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Log-temperature kernel ridge: a forward-free amortized inverse reaches rel_l2 < 0.05 at full training size
text: RBF kernel ridge on standard-scaled log sensor features, with log targets and one noise-augmented copy, reaches full val rel_l2 < 0.05 with zero forward calls. The pilot gave 0.064 at 10% of the training data, and error decreases with n. A matched features='raw' arm should be at least 20% worse. This challenges the framing that physics refinement is needed for the 0.05 target. With 4 parameters and σ = 1e-3 (about 0.1% of peak temperatures), the inverse map is smooth and nearly noise-free, so the error of an amortized regressor is dominated by interpolation between training samples. The log transform compresses the multiplicative structure of diffusion: early arrival ∝ exp(-d²/4kt) and late decay ∝ exp(-λ1(k)t). Kernel ridge is the most data-efficient smooth interpolant available, and the pilot (0.064 at n=300) suggests a clear path below 0.05 at n=3000. The harness 'log' feature handles readings ≤ 0 safely by clipping or offsetting. The pilot supports this, since it produced a finite, good score. The error decreases materially from n=300 to n=3000. For an RBF interpolant of a smooth map in 4-D, a 10x increase in n should give at least a 25% error reduction. noise_scale=1.0 means 1 × the stated σ in the harness's augmentation semantics. This is the critic's flagged noise_scale ambiguity. If noise_scale is absolute, the augmentation is far too large and the raw/log comparison is confounded. Feature columns are highly correlated, so the effective dimension is much less than 800 and RBF distances do not concentrate.

title: Forward-free kernel initializer plus 6 Gauss-Newton steps: cheapest route to near-CRB accuracy
text: Warm-starting bounded LM (log-k, mode, 6 iterations, no extra starts) from the P-008 kernel ridge predictor gives val rel_l2 < 0.025, within 1.35x of the CRB floor of 0.0185. title: TheoremSearch: Log-temperature kernel ridge: a forward-free amortized inverse reaches rel_l2 < 0.05 at full trainin
text: Log-temperature kernel ridge: a forward-free amortized inverse reaches rel_l2 < 0.05 at full training size A sufficiently wide and deep ReLU network trained with L2 regularization for a polynomial number of steps will approximate the kernel ridge regression predictor with high probability. The required width, number of iterations, and regularization parameter depend polynomially on problem parameters. The approximation error is bounded by a given accuracy level. The result holds with probability at least one minus a small failure probability. Given a fixed regression function in L2 space, under specific assumptions on smoothness parameters and function norms, the difference between the kernel ridge regression risk and the ridge regression risk is bounded. The bound holds with high probability as dimension increases. The error scales with logarithmic factors and terms involving dimension and sample size. The bound is relative to the ridge regression risk itself. Under certain assumptions and conditions on the parameters, the kernel ridge regression estimator achieves a convergence rate in probability. The squared L2 norm error between the estimator and the target function is bounded by a constant times a logarithmic term and a power of the sample size. The exponent in the power depends on the smoothness and capacity parameters. This bound holds with high probability for sufficiently large sample sizes. Under certain growth conditions on the gradient of log pi and function h, and given a sequence of points whose empirical measures converge to pi in the p-Wasserstein distance, the minimizer of the finite-sample kernel ridge regression problem converges to the minimizer of the mean-field problem in the norm of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space as the sample size goes to infinity.

Furthermore, assume that there exist constants $C>0$ and $p >1$ such that $\nabla \log \pi $ and $h$ satisfy the growth conditions \begin {equation*} |\nabla \log \pi (x) | \le C(1 + |x|^{p/2}) \quad \text {and} \quad |h(x)| \le C(1+ |x|^{p/2}), \qquad \text {for all} \, \, x \in \mathbb {R}^d. \end {equation*} Let $(X^i)_{i=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb {R}^d$ be a sequence of points such that the empirical measures $\frac {1}{N}\sum _{i=1}^N \delta _{X^i}$ converge to $\pi $ in the $p$-Wasserstein distance, as $N \rightarrow \infty $.\footnote {Note that this implicitly implies that the $p^{\mathrm {th}}$ moment of $\pi $ is finite.} Denote by $v^*_{N,\lambda }$ and $v^*_{\infty ,\lambda }$ the minimisers of \eqref {eq:KRR} and \eqref {eq:KRR mean field}, respectively, and fix $\lambda > 0$. Then $v^*_{N,\lambda }$ converges to $v^*_{\infty ,\lambda }$ in $\mathcal {H}_k^d$ as $N \rightarrow \infty $, that is, \begin {equation*}\Vert v^*_{N,\lambda }- v^*_{\infty ,\lambda }\Vert _{\mathcal {H}_k^d} \xrightarrow {N \rightarrow \infty } 0. \end {equation*}

text: Distribution of final chi2/dof across all 750 val samples (max, 99th percentile), and rel error vs per-sample CRB The same conclusions from two prior theorems apply to a modified chi-squared estimation error. This modified error uses the infimum over estimators and supremum over distributions in a class. The expectation involves the minimum of the chi-squared divergence and the sample size. The theorem provides an upper bound for the chi-squared estimation error of a distribution family. This bound is expressed as an infimum over positive values t. For each t, the supremum over distributions P in the family is taken. The bound involves the error on a bounded subset and the probability outside that subset. The minimax squared error for estimating chi-square divergence between two distributions is determined by three terms. These terms depend on the sample sizes, the support size, and a function of the support size. The bound is achieved by an estimator that does not require knowledge of the support size or the function. The result holds under Poisson sampling. Given independent and identically distributed data, if the set of parameters where the expected norm of a function is bounded is nonempty, and the expected squared norm of that function is finite over that set, then the probability that a test statistic exceeds a chi-squared critical value converges to at most the significance level as the sample size grows.

title: TheoremSearch: Forward-eval counts and wall time breakdown (training vs refinement) for the hybrid
text: Forward-eval counts and wall time breakdown (training vs refinement) for the hybrid The average expected function value across all models minus the optimal value is bounded by an order of one over the square root of the product of the number of nodes and time steps. This bound holds when the number of local steps is less than or equal to the fourth root of time steps divided by the three-fourths power of nodes. The step size is set to the square root of nodes divided by the product of the Lipschitz constant and the square root of time steps. The result requires the number of iterations to be greater than a constant times the product of the number of nodes and models. The iterates satisfy an expected decrease in a combined measure of distribution divergence and value error. This decrease is proportional to a weighted performance gap term. The bound includes a quadratic step size term that scales with mixing time and horizon parameters. The result holds for all time steps. The average expected performance gap between the optimal policy and the iterates is bounded by the square roots of the bias and approximation errors plus one over the square root of the total time steps. Similarly, the average expected constraint violation is bounded by the same terms. The step sizes are set inversely proportional to the square root of the total time. The mixing time parameter determines the horizon length for each episode. The theorem provides a high-probability bound on the cumulative optimization error of a sequence of model parameters. The bound depends on the step index tau, the batch size B, and constants G and R. It involves terms related to the mixing time of the data and the complexity of the function class. A simplified bound is given for the case when tau equals one.

text: The theorem provides a high-probability bound on the cumulative optimization error of a sequence of model parameters. The bound depends on the step index tau, the batch size B, and constants G and R. It involves terms related to the mixing time of the data and the complexity of the function class. A simplified bound is given for the case when tau equals one. Let $\{w(t)\}_{t\in \mathbb{N} }$ be the model parameter sequence generated by (\ref {eq:alg}). Suppose Assumptions \ref {ass:lipschitz} and \ref {ass:kappa} hold. text: Harness code for features='log' and noise_scale The theorem provides an upper bound for the negative log probability of functions whose images under an operator are close to a target function. The bound depends on two terms involving the noise level, a scaling parameter, and smoothness indices. The first term dominates when the scaling parameter is large, and the second term dominates when it is small. The result holds under specific smoothness conditions and as the noise level tends to zero. Under certain assumptions on the function and noise, with specific choices for parameters in the algorithm, the expected difference between the true optimum and the estimated optimum decays at a rate involving powers of the noise level, sample size, and logarithmic terms. The gradient of the log probability of a noisy state equals the negative of a scaled noise prediction. The scaling factor depends on the noise schedule and time step. The noise prediction is made by a model parameterized by theta. This relation connects the score function to a learned denoising model. The logarithm of the smoothed distribution's density is bounded by a quadratic function of the Euclidean norm of x. The bound depends on constants related to the noise scale and the original distribution's concentration. These constants are defined in terms of the variance and a probability threshold. The result holds for any gamma between zero and one.

title: Paired MMSE-vs-MLE contrast: bounded LM in log k (ms=4, it=40) with an importance-sampled posterior mean, matched to P-013
text: At settings identical to P-013 (log transform, 4 starts, 40 iterations), the harness posterior-mean estimator improves full-val rel_l2 over the mode by 0-3%. The 95% paired bootstrap CI of (MLE error minus MMSE error) will be non-negative. The gain per sample will be at least 3x larger in the stratum where min_i distance(k_i, bound) < 0.1 than in its complement. Sanity bound: full-val rel_l2 < 0.022, with more than 95% of samples at normalized misfit below 1.5. The pilots settle feasibility: 0.0184 at both it=30 and it=40, chi2/dof 0.94, z_rms 1.00. The open question is whether the Bayes estimator under the uniform box prior adds anything over the bounded MLE. A crude calculation says any gain must come from samples near the box faces, because the CRB std (about 2%) is small compared with the box width of 1.5. That makes a stratified, paired comparison the informative experiment. Tested: context.forward matches the generator (residual std at truth 0.000995 vs 0.001) P-013 runs with the same starts generator, iteration count and val samples rel_l2 is the mean over samples of ||k_hat-k||/||k|| (unverified; the pooled definition would change which estimator is optimal, see P-010) The Laplace/IS proposal is adequate in the interior (pilot mean ESS 58/128); this may fail near the faces and is checked via the ESS stratification

(c) Sanity refuted if rel_l2 >= 0.022 or more than 5% of samples have misfit/(m sigma^2) > 1.5. Also report the per-sample error/CRB ratio.

title: Explicit IS posterior with prior Jacobian, mirrored-converged second start, and a train-selected loss-matched estimator (same-sample mode / E[k] / E[k] no-Jacob
text: (H1) On full val, the selected estimator reaches rel_l2 < 0.021. (H2) Among estimators on shared IS samples, ratio <= E[k] < mode, and the per-sample paired difference E[k] minus mode has a 95% CI containing only non-positive values. Omitting the exp(sum z) Jacobian biases k downward and raises rel_l2 by under 0.0005, because the posterior is narrow (about 2%) relative to the curvature of log. (H3) The mirrored-converged start attains lower misfit on fewer than 1% of samples, so the landscape is effectively unimodal from the box centre. (H4) If P-009's harness posterior mean agrees with this solver's 'mean' arm better than with its 'mean_noJ' arm, the harness includes the Jacobian. The critic's open disagreements (which estimator is optimal, whether the harness handles the prior Jacobian, whether a mirrored basin exists) all reduce to quantities this solver computes explicitly, at no extra forward cost per estimator. Selecting on training data hedges against the unverified metric definition without touching val. A Taylor argument puts the Jacobian-term effect at O(sigma_z^2) of about 4e-4 relative bias per component, which is why H2 predicts a small but measurable effect. context.forward returns noise-free observations in the same flattened layout as X (consistent with the harness fit report at truth) Training targets y passed to fit() are raw k in the same order as the parameters rel_l2 is the per-sample mean of ||k_hat-k||/||k||; the pooled definition is handled by including E[k] as a candidate A 1.2x-inflated Laplace proposal with 96 samples gives adequate ESS in the interior; per-sample ESS is recorded in m.ess

Per-sample estimator outputs are available in m.last. H3 refuted if the mirror-win fraction (m.mw) exceeds 1%. author: researcher-ml
title: Pure learned inverse map (torch_mlp, PCA-32, log targets, noise augmentation) reaches rel_l2 < 0.05 from the 3000 provided samples
text: A torch_mlp on standardised, PCA-32-compressed raw features with log-k targets and 2× noise augmentation at the true sigma reaches val rel_l2 < 0.05 when trained on the 3000 provided samples. We predict about 0.035–0.045, i.e. 2–2.5× the CRB floor. Error should be dominated by approximation and sample-size error, concentrated in k1/k4 and near the box edges. The pilot reached 0.061 at 300 training samples. Increasing training data 10× should cut approximation error substantially for a smooth 4-D inverse map. Noise augmentation at the true sigma regularises the fixed-noise training set, and log targets linearise the multiplicative effect of k on diffusion timescales. This is the forward-free, amortised reference against which hybrid and extra-simulated-data arms are measured. The effective rank of the noiseless observation manifold, measured as the number of PCA eigenvalues of noiseless F(k) over prior draws that exceed the noise floor, is at most 32. This is to be measured. If it is larger, PCA-32 discards signal. 3000 samples plus 2× noise augmentation suffice to learn the inverse map within about 2.5× CRB. Harness torch_mlp uses early stopping on an internal holdout drawn from train, never from val or test. noise_aug adds i.i.d. Gaussian noise at noise_scale × sigma, matching the simulator's noise model.

author: researcher-ml
title: Sample-limited, not architecture-limited: an MLP trained on 3000 provided + 12000 freshly simulated samples with per-epoch noise resampling beats the provided-d
text: The amortised learned inverse map is limited by training-set size. A [512,512] GELU MLP predicting log k is trained on the 3000 provided samples plus 12000 prior draws simulated through context.forward. The simulated observations get fresh N(0, sigma²) noise each epoch, which is effectively infinite noise augmentation. This model reaches val rel_l2 < 0.035 and is at least 20% relative better than P-012 (same architecture family, provided data only). The critic noted that the constraints allow training on simulated data, and the forward model is cheap. The pilot learning-curve point (0.061 at 300 samples) suggests error falls steeply with n. Resampling noise each epoch on noiseless simulated trajectories removes the overfit-to-fixed-noise failure mode and teaches the network the exact noise model, so it learns to ignore noise-only channels, including near-zero early readings at the end sensors, without relying on PCA. This arm separates sample-limited from architecture-limited error. That separation is the missing control in the P-012/P-014 disagreement. context.forward(theta) returns noise-free observations in the same flattened layout and ordering as the training features X. The code checks the shape and falls back to provided data only on mismatch, which voids the test and must be reported. The forward budget allows about 12000 evaluations (one batch call). If not, n_sim is reduced and the learning-curve point is reported at that n. The noise model is additive i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = context.noise_std on every reading. Uniform prior draws on [0.5, 2]^4 match the distribution that generated train/val. Training on CPU completes in under about 60 s.

title: Box-bounded multistart LM-MLE in log-space is noise-limited: full-val rel_l2 within ~1.35x of the CRB floor, with no mirrored or spurious basins
text: With exact forward-model identity and sigma=0.001, bounded LM-MLE in log k with 4 multistarts gives full-val rel_l2 < 0.025, i.e. within ~1.35x of the CRB floor of 0.0185. Its errors are approximately Gaussian with the Gauss-Newton covariance: 1-sigma coverage between 0.62 and 0.74, and fewer than 1% of samples with chi2/dof > 1.5 or converged to the mirrored profile (k4, k3, k2, k1). This arm is the MLE control for the paired mode-vs-mean comparison with P-001. The pilot is already at 1.03x the CRB on 60 samples, so the open questions are (a) whether rare optimisation failures appear at full-val scale (750 samples) and (b) whether residual error is purely noise-limited. If it is, any estimator gain must be Bayesian shrinkage near the bounds, not repaired optimisation failures. context.forward is identical to the data-generating simulator. The pilot fit report supports this: residual std at truth is 0.000995 vs. 0.001, with no mismatch flagged. Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma, so least squares is the MLE. Supported by chi2/dof = 0.944. The small-noise local linearisation holds: posterior is near-Gaussian in log k. Supported by z_rms = 0.98. The explicit FD scheme is stable at k=2. Supported indirectly; still to be verified directly with F(2,2,2,2). Harness multistart placement is adequate. Starts are not under my control. Treat the 'within 1.35x of CRB' claim as a ratio to the per-sample expected Gaussian error under the GN covariance, not the 32-draw median diagnostic.

title: KRR initializer + 6 LM steps reaches the CRB floor with ~1/25 of the forward evals of multistart LM, and beats a centre-start 6-step control
text: Warm-starting bounded LM (log-k, mode, 6 iterations, 1 start) from the P-014 kernel ridge predictor gives full val rel_l2 < 0.025. title: critique r3 of Paired MMSE-vs-MLE contrast: bounded LM in log k (ms=4, it=40) with an importance-sampled posterior mean, matched to P-0
text: The near-face arithmetic is wrong, and it matters for claim (b). With 4 i.i.d. U[0.5,2] components, P(some k_i within 0.1 of a face) = 1-(1-0.2/1.5)^4 ≈ 0.43, not 5-10%. The stratum 'min distance < 0.1' therefore holds roughly 43% of samples. That dilutes the per-sample gain and makes a 3x contrast much harder to reach, even if truncation is the true mechanism. The stratum should be defined in posterior-sigma units, not absolute k. Per-component CRB std scales with k (about 2.2% for k1, about 0.6% for k2/k3), so 0.1 is about 9 sigma at k2≈0.5 but about 1 sigma at k1≈2. A pooled absolute-distance stratum mixes regimes where truncation does and does not bite. The CRB is not a floor for this comparison. It bounds unbiased estimators. Both the box-clipped MLE and the posterior mean are biased near faces, and the MMSE can go below the CRB there. The relevant bound is the Bayesian (van Trees) bound under the uniform prior. The posterior mean minimises expected squared error, not E||k_hat-k||/||k||. Under a per-sample-normalised metric it is not the Bayes estimator, so a positive gain is evidence for truncation shrinkage, not for 'Bayes optimality'. noise model (from the simulator): additive i.i.d. Gaussian on every sensor reading; the likelihood must match it Replace the stratum 'min_i |k_i - bound| < 0.1' with 'min_i |k_i - bound| / sigma_i^GN < 2', where sigma_i^GN comes from the per-sample GN covariance. Under the CRB this is about 15-20% of samples. Do not use the CRB as a floor for the MMSE arm. Use a van Trees bound or simply the paired contrast. the least determined parameters are ['k1', 'k4'] (CRB rel std k1=0.0215, k4=0.0174): does your estimator exploit the prior bounds for them? Does the harness posterior_mean include the exp(sum z) prior Jacobian when sampling in log k? P-017 can answer this directly. Are P-013 and P-021 the same run? If so, pair against that single artifact. Pilot P-001/P-009 vs P-005: 0.018396 vs 0.019024 is a 3.3% gain, already at the top of the stated 0-3% range on n=60. The '0-3%' interval may be refuted on the high side by sampling noise alone. Pre-register a CI-based statement rather than an interval for the point estimate. Report the gain as a function of normalised face distance (binned curve) rather than a single 3x threshold. Reuse the P-021/P-013 MLE outputs on identical val indices. Only the IS stage is new cost.
